title: Book 5
paragraphs: Accept the sacrifice of my confessions, offered by the ministry of my tongue, which you formed and stirred to confess to your name. Heal all my bones, and let them say, Lord, who is like you? For the one who confesses to you is not teaching you what is happening within him — a closed heart does not shut out your eye, nor can any man's stubbornness push back your hand: you dissolve it at your will, whether in pity or in judgment, and nothing can hide itself from your heat. But let my soul praise you, so that it may love you; and let it confess your mercies to you, so that it may praise you. Your whole creation never stops, never falls silent in praising you — not the human spirit, lifting its voice to you, nor creation, living or lifeless, through the voice of those who reflect on it — so that our souls may rise up out of their weariness toward you, leaning on the things you have created and passing through them to you, who made them wonderfully; and there is refreshment, and true strength.

Let the restless, the godless, depart and flee from you; yet you see them, and you split the darkness. And look — the universe is beautiful, even with them in it, foul as they are. And how have they wronged you? Or how have they disgraced your government, which, from heaven down to this lowest earth, is just and perfect? For where could they flee, when they fled from your presence? Or where do you not find them? But they fled so that they would not see you seeing them, and, blinded, might stumble against you — because you abandon nothing you have made — so that the unjust, I mean, might stumble against you, and be justly hurt, pulling away from your gentleness and stumbling over your uprightness and falling on their own roughness. Ignorant, in truth, that you are everywhere, you whom no place can contain! And you alone are near, even to those who remove themselves far from you. Let them turn, then, and seek you — because you have not abandoned your creation the way they have abandoned their Creator. Let them turn and seek you; and look, you are there in their heart, in the heart of those who confess to you and throw themselves upon you and weep in your embrace, after all their rough ways. Then you gently wipe away their tears, and they weep the more, and rejoice in weeping — because it is you, Lord — not a man of flesh and blood, but you, Lord, who made them — who remake and comfort them. But where was I, when I was seeking you? You were in front of me, but I had wandered away from you; I could not even find myself, how much less you!

I want to lay open before my God that twenty-ninth year of my life. There had come to Carthage a certain bishop of the Manichees, Faustus by name, a great snare of the devil — many were caught in that lure of his smooth language, which I admit I admired, even though I could separate it from the truth of the things I was eager to learn. Nor did I care so much for his skill as an orator as for the knowledge that this Faustus, so celebrated among them, was said to offer as food. His reputation had already declared him to be extremely learned in all valuable subjects and finely trained in the liberal arts. And since I had read and remembered a good deal of the philosophers, I compared some of their ideas with those long fables of the Manichees, and found the philosophers' account the more probable — even though the most they could manage was to pass judgment on this lower world; the Lord of it they could not discover at all. For you are great, Lord, and you look upon the humble, but the proud you see from a distance. You do not draw near except to the contrite in heart, and you are not found by the proud, no — not even if by their cleverness they could count the stars and the grains of sand, and measure the vault of heaven, and track the courses of the planets.

With the understanding and the wit you gave them, they search these things out, and they have discovered much; and, years in advance, they have foretold eclipses of those great lights, the sun and moon — on what day and hour, and to what degree — and their calculations did not fail; it happened just as they had foretold. And they wrote down the rules they had worked out, and these are still read today, and from them others foretell in what year, in what month, on what day, at what hour, and how much of its light, moon or sun, will be eclipsed — and so it comes to pass, exactly as foretold. People who do not know this art marvel at it and are astonished; those who do know it are exultant and puffed up; and, in an ungodly pride, falling away from you and losing your light, they foresee, long in advance, an eclipse of the sun's light that is going to happen — but they do not see their own, which is already happening. For they do not inquire, with any reverence, where they got the intelligence with which they search out these things. And though they find that you made them, they do not give themselves to you, to preserve what you made, nor do they sacrifice to you what they have made of themselves; they do not slay their own soaring imaginings, like birds of the air, nor their own prying curiosities — with which, like fish of the sea, they wander the unknown paths of the deep — nor their own indulgences, like beasts of the field, so that you, Lord, a consuming fire, might burn up those dead concerns of theirs and re-create them for immortality.

But they did not know the way — your Word — through whom you made these things that they count, and themselves who do the counting, and the sense by which they perceive what they count, and the understanding out of which they count; nor that of your wisdom there is no counting at all. But the Only Begotten has himself become wisdom for us, and righteousness, and sanctification, and was counted among us, and paid tribute to Caesar. They did not know this way by which to come down to him from themselves, and through him rise up to him. They did not know this way, and they thought themselves exalted among the stars, shining — and see, they fell to the earth, and their foolish heart was darkened. They say many true things about the created world, but they do not seek, with any reverence, the Truth who made the created world, and so they do not find him; or if they do find him, knowing him to be God, they do not glorify him as God, nor are they grateful, but they become foolish in their own thinking, and, calling themselves wise, they claim for themselves what is yours; and by this most perverse blindness they labor to blame on you what is really their own doing, inventing lies about you who are the Truth, and exchanging the glory of the incorruptible God for an image shaped like corruptible man, and birds, and four-footed animals, and creeping things — exchanging your truth for a lie, and worshiping and serving the created thing rather than the Creator.

Even so, I kept many true things about the created world from these men, and I saw the reasoning behind them from their calculations, the succession of the seasons, and the visible evidence of the stars; and I compared them with what Manichaeus had said, which in his madness he had written at great length on these very subjects — but I found in him no account of the solstices, or the equinoxes, or the eclipses of the greater lights, nor of anything of that kind I had learned in the books of secular philosophy. I was commanded, instead, simply to believe; and yet what I was told to believe did not match what had been established by calculation and by my own observation — it was, in fact, quite the opposite.

Does it please you, then, Lord God of truth, that a man knows all these things? Surely the one who knows all of this and does not know you is unhappy; but the one who knows you, even if he does not know these things, is happy. And the one who knows both you and these things is no happier for the sake of the things, but only for you — if, knowing you, he glorifies you as God, and is grateful, and does not become foolish in his thinking. Just as someone who knows how to own a tree, and gives you thanks for the use of it, is better off than someone who can measure the tree and count all its branches but does not own it, and does not know or love the one who created it — so too a believer, to whom this whole world of riches belongs, who, owning nothing, yet possesses everything by clinging to you, whom everything serves — even if he does not know the paths of the Great Bear, it is folly to doubt that he is in a better state than someone who can measure the heavens and count the stars and weigh the elements, and yet neglects you, who made everything in number, weight, and measure.

But then again, who told Manichaeus to write about these subjects too, when skill in them had nothing to do with piety? You have told man, Look here — piety and wisdom; of these other things a man could be ignorant and still have perfect knowledge of piety and wisdom. But these other things, since he did not know them, yet had the shameless nerve to teach them, make it plain that he could have had no knowledge of piety at all. For it is empty vanity to profess knowledge of worldly things even when it is genuine knowledge — but confession to you is piety. And so this wanderer talked at such length about these worldly matters for this reason: so that, once caught out by people who had actually learned them, it would become clear what kind of understanding he had of the deeper, more difficult matters. For he did not want to be thought little of, and he set about persuading people that the Holy Spirit, the Comforter and Enricher of your faithful, was present within him personally, with full authority. So when it was discovered that he had taught falsely about the heavens and the stars, and about the movements of the sun and moon — even though these things have nothing to do with the doctrine of religion — his sacrilegious presumption became plain enough to see, since he was teaching things he not only did not know, but had gotten wrong, with such an insane vanity and pride that he tried to claim them for himself, as though he were a divine being.

When I hear some Christian brother who is ignorant of these things, and mistaken about them, I can patiently watch such a man hold his opinion; I do not think any ignorance about the position or nature of the physical creation can hurt him, so long as he does not believe anything unworthy of you, Lord, Creator of all things. But it does hurt him if he thinks such things belong to the substance of the doctrine of piety, and insists too stubbornly on what he does not actually know. And still, such weakness, in the infancy of faith, is carried by our mother, Love, until the newborn believer can grow up into a mature man, no longer tossed about by every wind of doctrine. But as for the man who took it upon himself to be the teacher, the source, the guide, the leader of everyone he could persuade — so that whoever followed him believed he was following not a mere man but your Holy Spirit — who would not judge that such madness, once it was caught teaching anything false, deserved to be despised and utterly rejected? But I had not yet worked out clearly whether the alternation of longer and shorter days and nights, and of day and night themselves, along with the eclipses of the greater lights, and whatever else of that kind I had read about in other books, could be reconciled with what he said — so that, if it could be reconciled, it would still remain an open question for me whether it actually was so or not; but I might, on the strength of his supposed holiness, rest my trust on his authority.

For almost all of those nine years, during which my mind was unsettled and I was their disciple, I had longed too intensely for this Faustus to come. The rest of the sect, whoever I happened to run into, whenever they could not answer my objections about these matters, still held out the coming of this Faustus to me — through conversation with him, these and even greater difficulties, if I had any, were to be cleared up most easily and fully. So when he came, I found him a man of pleasant conversation, who could speak fluently and in better phrases — but still saying just the same things the others were in the habit of saying. But what good was the cupbearer's finest polish to my thirst for a more precious drink? My ears were already glutted with the same old stuff, and it did not seem any better to me for being better said, nor any truer for being eloquent, nor was the soul any wiser because the face was handsome and the language graceful. But the people who held him out to me were no good judges of such things, and so to them he seemed knowing and wise, because his words were pleasing. I had noticed, though, that another sort of people were suspicious even of the truth, and refused to accept it if it was delivered in smooth, abundant language. But you, my God, had already taught me, by wonderful and hidden ways, and so I believe you taught me — because it is the truth, and there is no teacher of truth besides you, wherever and however it may shine on us. From you, then, I had already learned that nothing ought to seem spoken truly just because it is eloquent, nor false just because the delivery is clumsy; nor true just because it is delivered plainly, nor false because the language is rich — but that wisdom and foolishness are like wholesome and unwholesome food, and elegant or plain phrasing is like fine or common dishes; either kind of food can be served on either kind of dish.

That eagerness, then, with which I had for so long looked forward to that man, was truly delighted by his manner and feeling as he argued, and by his choice and readiness of words to dress up his ideas. I was delighted, and, along with many others — more than they were — I praised and extolled him. It bothered me, though, that in the crowd of his listeners I was not allowed to bring forward and share, in familiar conversation with him, the questions that troubled me. When I finally could, and began, with my friends, to claim his attention at times when it was not improper for him to discuss things with me, and brought forward the matters that were troubling me, I found him, first of all, entirely ignorant of the liberal arts, except for grammar, and that only in an ordinary way. But because he had read some of Cicero's speeches, a very few books of Seneca, some of the poets, and whatever few volumes of his own sect had been written in Latin and written well, and because he practiced speaking every day, he had picked up a certain eloquence, which turned out to be all the more pleasing and seductive because it was guided by a good natural wit and a kind of native charm. Is this not how I remember it, Lord my God, judge of my conscience? My heart and my memory are before you, you who at that time were directing me by the hidden mystery of your providence, and were setting my shameful errors before my own face, so that I might see them and hate them.

Once it was clear that he was ignorant of the very subjects in which I had thought he excelled, I began to despair of his being able to open up and resolve the difficulties that troubled me — of which, in fact, he might still have held the truths of piety despite his ignorance, had he not been a Manichee. For their books are stuffed with endless fables about the heavens, the stars, the sun, and the moon, and I no longer thought him capable of deciding satisfactorily the question I most wanted answered: whether, comparing these things with the calculations I had read elsewhere, the account given in the books of Manichaeus was preferable, or at least as good. When I proposed that this be looked into and discussed, he, to his credit, shrank modestly from the burden. For he knew that he did not know these things, and he was not ashamed to admit it. He was not one of those talkative people, many of whom I had put up with, who undertook to teach me these things and said nothing. This man had a heart — not rightly turned toward you, but not altogether treacherous to himself either. He was not entirely unaware of his own ignorance, and he would not recklessly get himself tangled up in a dispute from which he could not retreat or extricate himself cleanly. I liked him the better for this. For the honesty of a candid mind is a finer thing than knowledge of the matters I wanted to learn — and that is how I found him, in all the harder and more subtle questions.

With my enthusiasm for the writings of Manichaeus blunted like this, and despairing even more of their other teachers, since he, so celebrated among them, had turned out this way on the very points that had perplexed me, I began instead to work with him on the literature he himself was devoted to — which I was at that time also teaching, as a professor of rhetoric, to the young students at Carthage — and to read with him, whether it was what he wanted to hear or what I judged suited to his talent. But all the effort I had meant to put into advancing in that sect, once I knew this man, came to a complete end — not that I detached myself from them entirely, but, finding nothing better, I settled to make do, for the time being, with whatever I had already fallen into, unless something more worth choosing should dawn on me. So Faustus, that snare of death to so many, had now, without meaning or knowing it, begun to loosen the knot in which I was caught. For your hands, my God, in the secret purpose of your providence, did not abandon my soul; and out of my mother's heart's blood, poured out in her tears night and day, a sacrifice was offered to you on my behalf; and you dealt with me by wonderful ways. You did it, my God — for a man's steps are ordered by the Lord, and he directs his path. Or how else could we obtain salvation, except from your hand, remaking what it made?

You dealt with me so that I would be persuaded to go to Rome, and to teach there instead of what I was teaching at Carthage. And how I came to be persuaded of this, I will not fail to confess to you, because here too the deepest recesses of your wisdom, and your most immediate mercy toward us, must be considered and confessed. I did not want to go to Rome because of the higher earnings and higher honors that my friends, who urged me to it, promised me — though even those things did have some influence on my mind at the time — but my main, almost my only, reason was that I had heard that students there studied more peacefully, kept in check under the restraint of stricter discipline, so that they did not, on a whim, rush impudently into the lecture room of a teacher they were not enrolled with, and were not even let in without his permission. Whereas at Carthage a shameful and unruly license reigns among the students. They burst in with wild, almost frantic behavior, and disrupt whatever order a teacher has set up for the good of his students. They commit various outrages with astonishing recklessness, outrages that would be punishable by law if custom did not protect them — and that custom only proves them more wretched still, since they now do as lawful what, by your eternal law, will never be lawful; and they think they get away with it, when in fact they are punished by the very blindness with which they do it, and suffer far worse than what they inflict. The habits, then, that I refused to adopt as a student, I now had to put up with, as a teacher, in others; and so I was glad to go where everyone who knew told me the same thing was not done. But you, my refuge and my portion in the land of the living, so that I might exchange my earthly dwelling for the salvation of my soul, prodded me at Carthage, to tear me away from it, and at Rome offered me enticements, to draw me there, using men in love with a dying life — the ones doing frantic things, the others promising empty ones — and, to correct my steps, you secretly made use of their perversity and my own. For both the people who disturbed my peace were blinded by a shameful frenzy, and the people who invited me elsewhere had the flavor of the earth about them. And I, who here despised real misery, went there in search of an unreal happiness.

But why I left from here and went there, you knew, God, though you showed it neither to me nor to my mother, who wept bitterly over my leaving and followed me all the way to the sea. But I deceived her — she was holding onto me by force, meaning either to keep me back or to come with me — and I pretended that I had a friend I could not leave until he had a fair wind to sail. And I lied to my mother — to such a mother — and got away. For this too you have mercifully forgiven me, keeping me, filled as I was with abominable defilements, safe from the waters of the sea, and bringing me to the water of your grace — so that once I was cleansed, the streams from my mother's eyes, with which she daily watered the ground under her face on my account, might be dried. And yet, refusing to go back without me, I barely persuaded her to stay that night in a place near our ship, where there was a chapel in memory of the blessed Cyprian. That night I secretly left, and she was not left behind in her weeping and praying. And what, Lord, was she asking of you, with so many tears, except that you would not let me sail? But you, in the depth of your counsels, hearing the real substance of her desire, paid no attention to what she was actually asking, so that you might make me what she was always asking for. The wind blew and filled our sails, and the shore dropped away from our sight; and she was there the next morning, frantic with grief, filling your ears with her complaints and groans, which you then disregarded — while, through my own desires, you were hurrying me on to put an end to all desire, and the earthly part of her love for me was disciplined by the scourge of sorrows she had been allotted. For she loved having me with her, as mothers do — but far more than most; and she did not know what great joy you were about to work for her out of my absence. She did not know; and so she wept and wailed, and in that agony there appeared in her the inheritance of Eve — seeking in sorrow what she had brought forth in sorrow. And yet, after accusing me of treachery and hard-heartedness, she went back to interceding with you for me, returned to her usual place, and I went on to Rome.

And there I was, struck down by the scourge of bodily sickness, and I was on my way down to hell, carrying with me all the sins I had committed against you, and myself, and others — many and serious sins, on top of that burden of original sin by which we all die in Adam. For you had not yet forgiven me any of these things in Christ, nor had he abolished, by his cross, the hostility I had incurred with you through my sins. For how could he, through the crucifixion of a phantom — which is what I believed him to be? So the death of my soul was every bit as real as I believed the death of his flesh to be false; and just as real as the death of his body actually was, that was how false the life of my soul was, in not believing it. And now, as the fever grew worse, I was passing away, departing forever. For if I had died then, where would I have gone, except into fire and torments, exactly as my misdeeds deserved under the truth of your judgment? And of this she knew nothing, yet even so, while absent, she prayed for me. But you, present everywhere, heard her where she was, and had compassion on me where I was, so that I might recover the health of my body, even though I was still crazed, in my sacrilegious heart. For in all that danger I did not so much as desire your baptism, and I had been better as a boy, when I begged for it from my mother's devotion, as I have already told and confessed. But I had grown up to my own shame, and I madly mocked the prescriptions of your medicine — you, who would not allow me, being what I was, to die a double death. Had my mother's heart been pierced by that wound, it could never have healed. For I cannot describe the love she had for me, and how much more violent her anguish in bearing me now, in the spirit, than it had been at my birth, in the flesh.

I do not see, then, how she could have been healed, if such a death of mine had struck through the depths of her love. And where would her prayers have gone — so strong, so unceasing, addressed to you alone? But would you, God of mercies, have despised the contrite and humbled heart of that chaste and sober widow, so generous in almsgiving, so full of devotion and service to your saints, never missing the offering at your altar, twice a day, morning and evening, without fail, coming to your church — not for idle gossip and old wives' tales, but so that she might hear you in your teachings, and you might hear her in her prayers? Could you have despised and rejected the aid she sought with her tears — tears with which she begged you for not gold or silver, nor any changeable or passing good, but the salvation of her son's soul — you, by whose gift she was the kind of woman she was? Never, Lord. Yes, you were there, listening and acting, in the order you had determined beforehand that it should happen. Far be it that you should have deceived her in your visions and answers — some of which I have mentioned, some I have not — which she stored up in her faithful heart, and, in her constant praying, pressed upon you as though they were your own signed promise. For because your mercy lasts forever, you condescend, to those whose debts you forgive completely, to also become a debtor through your own promises.

You cured me, then, of that sickness, and healed the son of your servant, for a time, in body, so that he might live for you to grant him a better and more lasting health later on. And even then, in Rome, I joined myself to those deceiving and deceived 'holy ones' — not only their ordinary disciples, one of whom was the man in whose house I had fallen sick and recovered, but also those they call 'the Elect.' For I still thought that it is not we who sin, but some other nature, I knew not what, sinning within us; and it flattered my pride to be free of blame, and, whenever I had done something wrong, not to confess that I had done it, so that you might heal my soul because it had sinned against you — but instead I loved to make excuses for it, and to accuse some other thing, I knew not what, that was with me but was not me. But in truth it was entirely me, and my own wickedness had divided me against myself. And that sin was all the more incurable because I did not judge myself a sinner; and it was a detestable wickedness that I would rather have you, you, God almighty, be defeated within me, to my ruin, than have myself be defeated by you, to my salvation. Not yet, then, had you set a guard before my mouth and a door of safekeeping around my lips, so that my heart would not turn aside to wicked speech, to make excuses for sin, along with men who work iniquity — and so I still remained joined to their Elect.

But now, despairing of making progress in that false teaching — even the parts of it I had resolved to settle for, if I found nothing better — I now held more loosely and carelessly. For a thought half rose up in me that those philosophers they call the Academics were wiser than the rest, because they held that a person ought to doubt everything, and maintained that no truth can be grasped by human beings — for, not yet understanding even their actual meaning, I too was fully convinced they held the view commonly reported of them. Yet I openly and freely discouraged that host of mine from the excessive confidence I saw he had in those fables the books of Manichaeus are full of. Even so, I lived in closer friendship with them than with others outside that heresy — though I did not defend it with my old eagerness. Still, my closeness to that sect — Rome secretly sheltering many of them — made me slower to look for any other way, especially since I had given up hope of finding the truth, from which they had turned me aside, in your Church, Lord of heaven and earth, Creator of all things visible and invisible; and it seemed to me quite unfitting to believe that you had the shape of human flesh and were bounded by the bodily outline of our limbs. And because, whenever I wanted to think about my God, I did not know what to think of except some mass of bodies — since anything that was not such a mass did not seem to me to be anything at all — this was the greatest, and almost the only, cause of my inescapable error.

And so I believed Evil, too, to be some such kind of substance, having its own foul and hideous bulk — whether something coarse, which they called earth, or something fine and subtle, like the substance of the air, which they imagine to be a kind of malignant mind creeping through that earth. And because a piety of sorts compelled me to believe that the good God never created any evil nature, I pictured two masses, opposed to one another, both unbounded, but the evil one narrower, the good one wider. And from this poisonous starting point, the other sacrilegious notions followed after me. For whenever my mind tried to turn back to the Catholic faith, it was driven off, since what I thought was the Catholic faith was not the Catholic faith at all. And it seemed to me more reverent to believe of you, my God — to whom your mercies give thanks out of my mouth — that you were unbounded, at least on other sides, even though on the one side where the mass of evil was set against you I was forced to admit you were bounded, than to imagine you bounded on every side by the shape of a human body. And it seemed better to me to believe that you had created no evil — which, in my ignorance, seemed to me not merely some substance but a bodily substance, since I could not conceive of mind except as a subtle body, diffused through definite spaces — than to believe that the nature of evil, as I conceived it, could come from you. And I believed that our Savior himself, your Only Begotten, had been reached out, as it were, for our salvation, out of the mass of your most radiant substance, so that I believed nothing of him except what I could picture in my own vanity. His nature being such as I imagined, I thought he could not have been born of the Virgin Mary without being mixed with flesh, and I could not see how what I had pictured to myself in this way could be mixed with flesh without being defiled. So I was afraid to believe he was born in the flesh, for fear I would be forced to believe he was defiled by the flesh. Your spiritual children will now smile at me, gently and lovingly, if they happen to read these confessions of mine. Yet that is exactly what I was.

Furthermore, whatever the Manichees had found fault with in your Scriptures, I thought could not be defended; and yet at times I did genuinely want to discuss these particular points with someone very well versed in those books, to see what he made of them. For the words of a certain Helpidius, as he spoke and argued face to face against the Manichees, had already begun to unsettle me back in Carthage — he had brought forward things out of the Scriptures that were not easily answered, and the Manichees' response to them seemed weak to me. And they did not care to give this response publicly, only to us in private. It was that the Scriptures of the New Testament had been corrupted by some person or other, wanting to graft the law of the Jews onto the Christian faith — yet they themselves never produced any uncorrupted copies. But I, conceiving of everything only in bodily terms, was mostly held down, violently oppressed and, in a way, suffocated by those 'masses' — and, gasping for the breath of your truth beneath them, I could not breathe it in pure and untainted.

I began, then, diligently to practice what I had come to Rome to do — teach rhetoric — and first to gather some students at my house, people to whom, and through whom, I had begun to become known. And then I found other, different offenses being committed in Rome, ones I had not been exposed to in Africa. It was true that the 'wreckings' carried out by wild young men were not practiced there, as I had been told — but suddenly, so they told me, in order to avoid paying their teacher's fee, a group of young men would plot together and transfer to another teacher — breakers of faith, who for love of money hold justice cheap. My heart hated these people too, though not with a perfect hatred; perhaps I hated them more because I was the one about to suffer from them than because they were doing something utterly wrong. Such people are, in truth, base, and they go whoring away from you, loving these fleeting mockeries of temporal things and filthy profit, which dirties the hand that grabs it — clinging to the fleeting world and despising you, who endure, and call back, and forgive the adulterous soul of man when she returns to you. And now I hate such twisted, depraved people, though I still love them if they are capable of correction, enough to want them to prefer learning to money, and to prefer you, God, the truth and fullness of certain good, and the purest peace, to learning itself. But at the time, I disliked their wickedness more for my own sake than I wished them well for yours.

So when the people of Milan sent to Rome, to the prefect of the city, asking him to supply them with a teacher of rhetoric for their city, sending him even at public expense, I put in an application — through those very people, drunk on Manichaean vanities, from which I was about to be freed, though neither of us knew it — that Symmachus, then prefect of the city, would test me by setting me some subject, and then send me. I came to Milan, to Bishop Ambrose, known throughout the world as one of the best of men, your devoted servant, whose eloquent preaching regularly served out to your people the finest of your wheat, the gladness of your oil, and the sober intoxication of your wine. I was led to him without knowing it was you leading me, so that through him I might come to know you and be led to you. That man of God received me like a father, and showed me the kindness of a bishop on my arrival. From then on I began to love him — not at first as a teacher of the truth, which I had entirely given up hoping to find in your Church, but simply as a man who was kind to me. And I listened attentively to him preaching to the people — not with the intention I should have had, but, in a way, testing his eloquence, to see whether it lived up to its reputation, or ran fuller or thinner than I had been told — and I hung on his words with close attention, but as for the substance, I was an indifferent and scornful onlooker; and I took pleasure in the sweetness of his speaking, which was more learned, though in manner less winning and appealing, than Faustus's — but as for substance, there was no comparison, for the one was wandering among Manichaean delusions, while the other was teaching salvation in the soundest way. But salvation is far from sinners, such as I still was as I stood before him; and yet I was drawing nearer, little by little, and without knowing it.

Even though I took no trouble to learn what he was saying, and only cared how he said it — since that empty concern was all that was left to me, having given up hope of any path open to man toward you — even so, along with the words I would have chosen, the substance I would have rejected also made its way into my mind; I could not keep the two apart. And while I opened my heart to let in how eloquently he spoke, there also entered how truly he spoke — though this happened gradually. For, first of all, these matters, too, had now begun to seem to me defensible; and the Catholic faith, against which I had thought nothing could be said in answer to the Manichees' objections, I now thought could be maintained without embarrassment — especially after I had heard one or two passages of the Old Testament explained, and often 'in a figure,' which, when I had understood them literally, had killed me spiritually. So, once a great many passages from those books had been explained, I now blamed my own despair, for having believed that no answer could be given to those who hated and mocked the Law and the Prophets. Even so, I still did not see that the Catholic way was to be held simply because it too could find learned defenders, able to answer objections at length and with some show of reason; nor that what I held was to be condemned simply because both sides could be defended. For the Catholic cause did not, to me, seem defeated — only not yet victorious.

At this point I turned my mind earnestly toward finding whether I could somehow, by some certain proof, convict the Manichees of falsehood. If I could once have conceived of a spiritual substance, all their strongholds would have been knocked down and cast entirely out of my mind — but I could not. Even so, concerning the structure of this world, and the whole of nature reachable by the senses of the flesh, the more I thought about and compared things, the more probable I judged the views of most of the philosophers to be. So, in the manner of the Academics, as they are commonly thought to have held — doubting everything, and wavering among all positions — I settled to this extent: that the Manichees were to be abandoned. I judged that, even while doubting, I could not remain in that sect, to which I already preferred some of the philosophers; yet to those philosophers, since they were without the saving name of Christ, I absolutely refused to entrust the cure of my sick soul. I determined, then, to be a catechumen in the Catholic Church, to which I had been commended by my parents, for as long as it took, until something certain should dawn on me, showing me which way to steer my course.
